title: Working with King Oliver: band, habits, seating, bandstands and hobbies
summary: Dodds recalls joining Oliver's band in 1921, comparing it to Fate Marable's, and describes Oliver's size, appetite, mutes, dress, call numbers, blues tempos, band seating, bandstand acoustics, hobbies, and early work with George Thomas. This is one indivisible block.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Okay, it's going. Baby, since Joe Oliver isn't around anymore, I thought I'd ask you a few questions about Oliver and his band. At the time you knew him, that you played with him, how did you enjoy working with the band? Well, Bill, as far as the band's concerned, it was a swell band to work with. Everybody knew what they were doing, everybody was set with anything went off, everybody was ready. When did you join the Oliver band? Well, I joined the Oliver band by the year of 1921. I left the Stuckford's line in 20 and Joe Oliver sent for me to come to Frisco and we worked on Marcus Street. At the Jitna Dance Hall. And that's where I come in contact with Joe Oliver. Who else was in the band when you joined? Well, there were Henri Dutre, trombone, with my brother John Clannett and Eddie Garland on bass file. I'm forgetting that. Oh, the piano player was Bill. And we had Dave Jones playing sax. Did he play mellophone ever with the band too or just the sax? No, he didn't play mellophone with the King Alva outfit as with the Fade Marable outfit. How did the band compare with the Fade Marable band? There's no comparison because we had more men in the Fade Marable band. There's more harmony. And, uh, well, quite naturally, you know, in any, any band that, uh, that's an orchestra like that, the more men you got, the better music you got. That's the way I feel. Now, I haven't got to work the same way, hasn't got to be the same way. That's the way I feel. I feel that you have more men, you can bring more harmony out. The man has got the stick completed for the melody. And with the harmony out of the band, that makes a good band, I think. Um, how did the bands compare in their, uh, or the people that, how did, how were they received? That is, the public reception. Oh, the reception of the public was very good. And for which one? You mean, which is best, do you think? Or could you compare? Well, I think, I think that the, comparing the sets of people, I think the people that we had on the boat was a much better set of people. Because they danced. Yeah. And they danced everything. And I'm going to tell you a little something, Bill, about your home. We passed through Hanover, Missouri. I think I told you about that. How nobody danced. Oh, yeah. And then when they, when they, when they, we was almost ready to stop playing. Well, about, we almost knocked, couldn't work about 1130. And, uh, this was about 11 o'clock. People started dancing. And good grace, we couldn't give them enough. It was just dance, dance, dance. We had to make an extra trip out of Hanover. That I will never forget. What'd they do, stand around and listen to the French? They stand around and listen. Did they like it, you think? But just... That I didn't understand. I didn't understand. Why was it, why did they look? But, uh, still, I put two and two together within myself and figured this. But they just wasn't used to dancing by Negroes music. And that made a big difference. People are funny anyway. If they don't, regardless if they know anything is good, but it's not from the type of people, or whom the people that they care to, to dance for, or dance with, or enjoy their music, they don't do it. But I don't think it meant any different. Only, it was just surprising to them to have a Negro band there. And I don't know if there's very much prejudice in Hanover, in Hanover, or St. Joe. I don't know if there's very much prejudice there. But I know they didn't dance. And we had to make an extra trip out of them. Had to make an extra trip. And that St. Joe, I think we had a little trouble in St. Joe, too. Missouri. Because the people that was very slow were dancing there. When they had no trouble in Kirkuk, they flocked right in. Very nice, nice crowd of people. Still, we would look the barn like we was wild or crazy or something. Well, that's big time. And I don't believe the people meant that, but just, it was something new to them, that's all. Yeah. Well, at the Royal Garden with Oliver here in Chicago, did they dance there a good deal? Oh, did they dance? Well, actually, all I had to do was make people continue to dance. We'd be playing a number, we'd go down very soft, and I would use sandpaper. Just like, shh, shh, shh. You really used sandpaper in your hand? We used sandpaper. And people would dance by that sandpaper. Just two pieces together sliding? Yeah, just two pieces. Just sliding. And people would dance by that. That's soft. That's how soft we went. Yeah. And people would dance perhaps half hour like that. Fifteen minutes. Um, to get back to Joe Oliver now, I'd like to find out, nobody tells us much exactly what kind of a fellow he was, even how tall was he? Can you think it's Bill Johnson? Well, oh, he was taller than Bill. Taller than Bill Johnson. So he must be close to six feet, maybe. Just about, I think. And, uh, about five foot and nine, something like that. I know he's a tall man. And he weighed 230 pounds. 230. He's quite a big man. And, uh, he was alright as long as you don't cross him. Yeah. He's like anyone else. If you cross him well then, he's pretty mean. Not particularly, not particularly weight anyone, but he was, he was talking very bad, very rough to you. I never had much trouble with him. Some people did. Um, what about his eating? People have told me he was a big eater. You hear those stories. Is that really true? Yes, Bill. Very true. I tell you, he came over to my house once, and, uh, the wife cooked him. Not particularly him, but she cooked a lot of potatoes, a lot of biscuits. And he, uh, cooked a small, small small-sized dishpan. Full. He, and he come down there eating them all. And he would drink, he drank a, a galvanized, uh, two-gallon bucket. Full of, full of juice. Which was made up as, uh, as, uh, lemonade. Yeah. Was that on the job or at home with the dinner? No, at home. At home with the dinner? What did they drink? Did he drink much liquor? Or beer? Or hard liquor ever? No, not in late years. He didn't drink very much. What do you mean by late years? Now, when you knew him, or? When I first knew him, he used to drink an awful lot. And I used to drink with him. That was back in, back in New Orleans? Yeah, back in New Orleans. He could drink anybody's pint. That's where he drank. And he wouldn't give you any of his, either. If he wanted to drink, he'd buy and drink for himself. That was a pint of whiskey. He would drink that. Drink the whole thing. I used to get next to him sometime. And, and take one drink out of it. That's all he'd let me have. Um, what about, um, on the job, you hear stories about having a big bucket there of lemonade or something, or sugar water and things of that kind. Do you remember? Well, yes, well that was, uh, not all the time. Cause, but he liked plenty of water. Drink plenty of water. And quite naturally he wanted to be something sweet, lemonade or something like that. So, he's a great fellow. Only one thing about him. I'm sorry I didn't do it. I'm sorry today that I didn't go back. He wanted me to play with him. I left him in, uh, in 24. The band busted up. And, uh, he came back in, 34. The place I was working, up on, uh, Michigan in, in 51st. Came in and asked me to join a band. That's when the band was, it was on a truck. Yeah. Going, uh, touring around. Yeah, going from town to town. But he had a bus he had bought. And, uh, he asked me would I join a band. It was a bunch of youngsters. He said, uh, it would be good for the kids' morale if I'd join a band. But I had quit myself. He didn't find me. I had quit myself. And so I just wouldn't take any more chances. Cause I was away, I just let it be that way. Yeah. And then again, I was with my brother. He had to make a living. In regards to Joe, he had to make a living so I stayed with him. Yeah. But that's one mistake that I think I made. I should have gone back to him. I don't think he played very long after that. No, he didn't. He didn't play very long before he died. A couple more years and he faded out. How was his lip when you knew it? Was he powerful? Well, I didn't hear him play. No, I mean in the, when you first joined him, was he, oh yes. Was he unusually loud or, uh? He wasn't unusually loud because he used a mute to mute himself down. Oh my God. And what kind of a mute did he usually use? A metal. Metal mute. Just a little, was it one of those little, uh, ones that looks something like a light bulb? Yeah. A little con mute, people told us. That's right. He didn't use any big, uh, uh, mute that stuck out in front of the horn or a rubber plunger? Did he use that ever? Well, he used that on top of this metal mute. A rubber plunger sometime on top of it. Yeah, sometime, yeah. Uh, I've heard too that he had a sugar can or something. He'd used a tin can. Did he ever use that? Well, in front. To my knowing, I, I, I forgot. I'd rather not say so. Yeah. What about a derby hat? Did he ever? Well, very suddenly he used that. He would use that occasionally. That was something he wanted to have this, this, uh, heavy sound. Yeah. Well, he would use that. Now, while we're talking about hats, can you tell anything about how he was dressed? How did he usually dress? Was he neat or did he, uh? Always very neat to be a big man. Very neat. Very neat. Was it the style to wear a derby in those days or not? I don't even remember. Yes, it was the style. Did he ever wear the derby then? Yeah, cause I had one myself. Yeah, it was style. Mm-hmm. And, uh, well, he's such a big man. He wasn't out of proportion, but just, he, he was so big. Yeah. Um. Looked like he's willing to try a trumpet. He's such a big man and he had a trumpet. He usually used a cornet, I guess, in those days, didn't he? A little... No, not particular. Uh, last, last ten or fifteen years, he used trumpet. Used trumpet. Uh-huh. Uh, what kind of uniforms did the, did the band, or how did you all dress? Say, at the Royal Garden, for instance? We had no uniforms. No uniforms. Only in the wintertime, we'd used tuxedos. Tuxedos. Tuxedos all winter. And the whole band dressed the same, the leader dressed the same as the others. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Exactly. Yeah. Um. Let's see, uh, anything else about, uh, Joe? That is, when he talked, uh, did he talk sort of soft, or was he loud spoken, or what? Did he talk a whole lot, or was he sort of a quiet man? Well, no, he was a man who was, had a joke to say all the time. He was kidding and joking all the time. Uh-huh. And, uh, he wasn't a very loud spoken man. He speak in proportion. He never howled at anybody, nothing like that. And, uh, well, he didn't have too much to say unless there's, uh, something for the band, or something for someone to do. Uh, in proportion. He wasn't a man to talk out of proportion. And, uh, his voice was not a proportion. I thought, to my, to my submission, I thought Joe Oliver was a very fine man. Did he have his family with him when he was here, with his wife here? I think so. I think so. His family was here. His daughter. I think his daughter got married here. Uh, she used to be a friend to my nieces and nephews. I don't, I don't know of her. Yeah. Uh, when the band would start a piece, did he, uh, stomp off, or did he sometimes start playing without the... Sometimes he'd have a pickup of two notes or three notes, or, uh, uh, staccato, staccato part, something like that, and Lloyd would join his, his notes. Sometimes he'd just start out by himself then, without the band? Sometimes, that's right. Uh, when he would call a number, say if you were gonna play, well, all I can think of is Royal Garden Blues, would he, uh, uh, give the title to you, or would he maybe just play a couple notes first, softly, like sometimes they do to tell you the tune? Well, perhaps, perhaps he, perhaps he would, he'd tell you what he's gonna play, and, uh, call the numbers out. They would, numbered like, uh, from, uh, one to one hundred, two hundred, like that, he'd call the number out, and you'd get it that way. And when he'd start off, sometime he'd kick it off, and sometime he'd pick up maybe a two note pickup, a one note pickup. I think that's got one note pickup, isn't it? Yes, yes, a one note pickup. Yeah, I don't remember exactly how it goes. It's either one note pickup, or the trumpet, or the trombone picks it up. Did you all play many requests for people, or did, uh, did you have, say at the Royal Garden did you arrange a whole set before you say we were gonna play about a half a dozen numbers? Did he figure out what they were gonna be, or did he just wait? No, he was just waiting. Now he was just waiting until the time presented itself in the play, and he was picking the stack from, he'd get, I'll tell you, he worked this one to one hundred, maybe, or one to three hundred, whatever he had, in his left drawer, and he would pick out the numbers all the way down, from one to so on. And, uh, sometime he'd go over, so on that set, we'd go back, and repeat. But it was a very seldom way to repeat the number. Very seldom. Well, did you, uh, a lot of the bands in New Orleans, and remember how Bunk's band used to do, they'd play a piece twice. If there had any applause at all, they'd play it over again right away. Did he still do that down there quite a bit? Did you, did Oliver do that much, or ever? Well, yes, he did it sometime. But, uh, perhaps we'd have a, uh, uh, repertoire, a repertoire for the night, and he'd have so many, so many numbers to play. And perhaps, uh, during the encores of those numbers, we didn't go back. Because through the night, we had so many numbers, we'd play them. Not particularly, but we would have those many numbers out. Yeah. Playing encores, sometimes you wouldn't get half of them. According to the encores, you played. He, he had, uh, he conducted the band pretty nice. Mm-hmm. About how long did, uh, did most pieces last? About as long as on the record, that's about three minutes? Or did you play them, maybe five or ten minutes sometimes? Well, that depends. That depends on how it was received, and, uh, maybe if we have enough applause, we'd play it back. Well, that was according to him. Mm-hmm. In other words, according to his mind, too. Yeah. Did you ever play the blues, uh, just, uh, improvised blues very often, or? Very, very, very often. And would that, uh, likely run longer, or shorter than the other numbers, or? None that particular. It was up to Joe what he wanted to do. Yeah. What tempos did you use for blues? Pretty slow or fast? Slow tempos. And sometime we'd speed it up just a little for, just the benefit of it making sound different, or something. Yeah. But all blues are slow tempos, Bill. Yeah, they should be, I know. Well, I don't, I don't, I wouldn't say that, none particular. And since I've known better about blues, it hasn't got to be particularly slow, but, uh, you get more, more into them when you're playing in the school. And that's the way blues supposed to be played anyway. Yeah. Like I see these guys with this rock and roll. That ain't nothing but blues. No, that's right. It's fast. Jumped up blues. They think they got something, but that's all that is. I think we'd play blues about mostly all tempos. You'd play as many waltzes, what's the difference? Did you play many waltzes at the Royal Garden or Dreamland? It was, it was practically a dance hall, see. We'd play a string of, of, of numbers, mix them in, Foxtrot, fast and blues. Do you remember this old waltz, Oh How I Miss You Tonight? Did you play that there? Do you remember Joe playing that? Well, we didn't play that for the dance. That may not have been out much in 1923. This was out. About that time. It was out. Cause I heard later that it was almost like a theme song or something. Yeah. Big hits he made out of it. Tell me something else. You've, in the past, you've told me the seating of the band, how the drums are on one end and the trombone, trumpet and so on, and ends up with the bass on the other. That's right. Did you all sit that way at the Royal Garden and? Yes. All in one line. You weren't, you didn't have like some nowadays they call the front line, put the trumpet and clarinet up and then the drums and bass in back. You didn't do that. Cause it's an unbalance. And you, while you've been on the ones that know that. You take a drum and sit in the middle of your outfit, unless you've got your band built around in a circle, it's not going to balance. And that's why these guys don't get, don't get the right balance of the band. Or you can take it and make it a record. You balance the band, put some over here and some over there and the heavy part of your instruments over that. It don't balance right. I'll tell you one experience where you can think about it. When we was writing in New York at the Stuyvesant. You remember we had a time balancing band on? Yeah. And let you, instrumentation was set right where they didn't balance. After all we had to get in the back of the hall, remember? Yeah. And that two double ceiling, that didn't go. Low ceiling and high ceiling. When you played at the Dreamland or Pekin you also sat always in a straight one long line then, when possible? Yeah, practically. We tried to have everybody on the same roof and on the same level. Yeah. That makes a big difference. The drummer didn't, the drummer didn't get up high on a little platform or anything in the back. No. And the piano was right in the line too then usually? Yeah. Yeah. What did you do about intermissions? Where did you, did the band stay on the stand? No, they would get down and stretch our legs and walk around, go outside, smoke. I've seen the time that it was customary of the band enough to sit on the stand and smoke. You had to get off the stand. How high was the stand at the Royal Garden? Well it was about four feet. Oh, higher, higher than the bed here for instance? Yes. It would be higher. Yeah, they would go up steps. Go up a few steps. And it wasn't too high, it was about, it reached a person's head level. Almost up to the... Yeah, it reached almost to the person's head level. When you were sitting down, you're hip. Yes. For the simple reason, Bill, a lot of people wouldn't understand that. But here's the reason. When your music is up over a person's head, now you may think of this, your music is above a person's head, it's a more even music. When it's up, and then you hit the ceiling and come down, it's not even. Well, what did you think about those real high band stands they have in New Orleans, sometimes up on like balcony, you know, second floor almost? That is still alright because it hits the ceiling, then it comes down from people. Well, if you hear that all over well, it balances itself. The Economin Hall in New Orleans has got that. Yeah, I remember the artesian hall. Yeah, the band sounds like it's way out of town over here. There's a story about that. A lot of people don't know today why that is. Who sticks up the place? That's the way the music sounds. You mean at the Economy Hall, it sounded... Anywhere. Where did it sound out of town? You mean it sounded softer or what? No, it just sounded like it's way away someplace. Sounds too far away. Oh, you mean when the band stand isn't right? Yeah, when it's not right. When it's up too high, or maybe up too low, down too low. Now you can hear a band down low, but you can't way up too high. A lot of musicians don't know that. A lot of leaders don't know that. The next thing, a lot of leaders come in the hall and they just sit anywhere. I don't know if that's what I could. Yeah. You don't pick a place to hear the acoustics of the place, and hear how it sounds, how the bands sound, and the sound better here than they went over here, or sound much better than they do there than over there, all that's in it. And that's what makes a lot of fellas' band don't sound together. That's the reason. It's an instrumentation. I'll tell you a place where we had a lot of trouble. Remember we went to work for Columbia? Was it Columbia? No. Victor. Oh yeah. Remember in New York? Yeah, I remember that street, yeah. You remember all the guy put a bucket of sand, gets some bass drum and mattress and something. Mattress and something like that. You see, that's the reason of that. You have to find out what acoustics of this place to make this band sound out there. So to get back to Joe Oliver now, at the intermission time did he mix with the other fellas, or did he try to sort of stay by himself? Was he just one of the boys, or how did he act? Sometimes. Sometimes he'd have a plan to set, an outfit, then again he would go by himself. Well, I can understand it now. Those days I didn't understand it. Now I understand it. It's like Bunker's just trying to do it. He tried to do the same thing, going by himself. Well, it's a whole lot to that. A lot of people can't have a bunch of men to talk natural with. They feel like any boss man. Yeah. He can't sit and chat with his workers, with his outfit. Get to himself. To me now, it doesn't make any difference. It's just what you talk about. You can't laugh and joke with your coworkers like that, because they'll get so they won't pay attention to you. Yeah. Well, you can't pass jokes with them like one another can. Well, I think of it, what hobbies or what interests, other interests did Joe Oliver have? Did he in sports or what did he do in his spare time? Of course, maybe that's none of our business, but still, I mean, I just wondered if he... That's all right. He was a baseball fiend. Baseball. Oh, he knew every baseball player that ever played. He knew them all. Well, for a fact, the whole band did. Your brother was that way too, wasn't he? Yeah, he was a fan too. Well, what about you? Were you that much of a fan? Not quite. Not until today. I see a player, I don't like him, but that's why he's just another player to me. Yeah. And he may do something good. All right. Somebody else thought he'd do something good too. Now what you gonna do with that guy? Yeah. That's mine. And next thing about it, I feel that it takes nine men to make a ball team. Now regardless of what I can do, I'm more than another body. That's me. Yeah. I feel the same way with the orchestra. It takes seven of us, or nine of us, or six of us to be in that orchestra. Now every man counts. You don't find many fellows said that. No. No. Well, that's where I am. Without those other guys, I can't do nothing. That's the sense. And I can't be no band by myself. That's the sense. And nobody else can. Now regardless of how much he can do, or what solos he does, he still ain't the band. Without that band, you still haven't got nothing. You got to have instrumentation and accordion. I played two piece band. I played three pieces. I played four pieces. I played five pieces. I played eight. I played twelve. I played sixteen. I had played twenty-five. But each one of those people that you got, that I fit, belongs to. Each one of them plays a part. I can't see why one guy can break up a band. He can't. Not if you don't want him to break up. Of course, one man is an awful asset to a band. He can be a soloist. Some of us can play, but they can't be a soloist. You know that to be a fan. Well, about Joe Oliver, was there any other hobbies he had? In New Orleans, they tell about him playing pool quite a bit. Did he do that? Yes, he was a pool player. He loves to play pool. He did up here too, then, in Chicago and San Francisco. Yes, when there were pool rooms. Well, you know in Chicago, we haven't got many pool rooms. No, that's what I know. And guys don't hang around the pool room all day. They'd play cards, something like that, but Joe Oliver wasn't much of a card player. My brother, he'd play cards. But I didn't play much cards, so there wasn't nothing good there. Deutra didn't play cards, so there was nothing doing there. So it's just different things that one can, you can't accomplish these things on a job. On a job that you're lonesome, well, some guy comes and plays some cards, well, then you do it just to do that part of the time away, but you're not fond of it. And the truth about it, Bill, there's a very few sports that I am really fond of. Sounds funny, but I never cared too many for different sports. I like baseball, I like football, I like all sports, but just for me to participate in it, I have to play baseball. This is something you may not know. Yeah, I wonder if you told me. And the batter, John and me, pitch and catcher. Pretty nice. And Johnny was the pitcher. No, he was the catcher. Catcher and you were the pitcher. Yep. But otherwise, my kids get out and play. I used to play pitch and catch when I was a kid, but not as much as you see other kids. Where did you play ball? Here in Chicago then? No, I didn't play ball. I played in New Orleans. On the satellites. Yeah. But my, one of my real hobbies was, a kite. A kite, flying a kite. Flying a kite. That's one of that. And another one was shooting marbles. Mm-hmm. There was a great hand for shooting marbles, and a great hand for flying a kite. And while I used to do other sports of kids, hop, scop, leap frog, and like that. Well, this blues that Richard M. Jones wrote, was it? New Orleans hop, scop, no, Thomas. George W. Thomas. New Orleans hop, scop blues. Was that any special game there, more than other parts? Yes. It wasn't more, but it was a game of kids. Uh, well that's a fellow, a very good friend of mine. I understand he's dead now. George, uh. George Thomas. George Thomas. You knew him. Very well. He's one of my first guys that hired me around, around in the district at that time. Piano and drum. That's where I was through the first time. Where did you work with him? Uh, one of those big houses, I don't remember now which one. One of the big houses, like Lula White's house, it wasn't her house, but similar to that. One in the red light district? Yeah. Wasn't in a place like George, a few clothes or... No, no. Or a cabaret in a house? No. What did you use, drums and piano? Drums and piano. That was all. That was pretty versatile. Yeah. You know you've got to learn that the same as any other thing? Different beats to the drum and piano? It's not easy. Those things, well I had all that to learn when I was coming up. And that's why I was so versatile. I could make a little band two or three people.
